summary: The SIP Identity header identifies the originator of a request, but STIR has no way to learn the identity of the called party. This Standards Track document updates prior guidance on that connected identity problem to match changes in SIP identity.

eli5.summary: Caller ID tells you who is calling, but you also want proof of who actually picked up.

questions: how to stop forged sip bye messages
subtitle: How the person you call can prove, in a signed token, that they are really the party you meant to reach.

tldr.problem: STIR signs who is calling, but nothing tells the caller who actually answered. Attackers can hijack the route of a number, or forge mid-call messages such as BYE.
tldr.mechanism: The answering side signs a new PASSporT type called rsp, carried in the Identity header of SIP responses and later requests. The signature covers the called party's identity, and diversion (div) PASSporTs explain any retargeting.
tldr.outcome: Callers can detect calls retargeted to an impersonator and reject forged mid-dialog or dialog-terminating messages, but only if the far side supports it and the caller's policy requires it.

today: RFC 9970 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2026. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Connected Identity Is Needed
sections.content:
STIR (RFC 8224) lets a SIP call carry a cryptographic assurance of who is calling. That blocks impersonation, which is behind robocalls, swatting, vishing and voicemail hacking.

The mirror-image problem is the identity of the party who answers. It can differ from the number dialed for harmless reasons such as call forwarding. But an attacker can also hijack the route of a called number and send the call to a resource they control. The lack of mutual authentication also lets outsiders inject forged messages, such as a BYE, into a SIP session.

Telling the caller who was reached is called connected identity. RFC 4916 did this for the older Identity mechanism of RFC 4474, partly by letting the From header change in the backwards direction. This document adapts the idea to STIR now that RFC 8224 has replaced RFC 4474. Its scope is two-party calls only; conferencing is left for future work.
sections.eli5: Imagine phoning a bank and having no way to know whether the person who answers really works there. Connected identity gives the answerer a way to show proof.

sections.title: The Problem Statement
sections.content:
The text names three situations where connected identity helps.

  • Redirected calls. Adversaries can redirect calls on the PSTN, and on the Internet there is no centralized or federated routing system for telephone numbers, so call routing can be arbitrary. Call centers for finance, healthcare and emergency services are named as attractive targets.
  • Forged mid-dialog requests. SIP has always allowed an intermediary to forge a BYE in the backwards direction. The RFC cites "call stretching" mobile fraud, where an intermediary makes one side think a call ended while the other side still sees it as active, creating a billing discrepancy.
  • Two-factor authentication. Telephone numbers are widely used for two-factor authentication, and connected identity assures the caller that they reached the phone for the called number.

There are limits. Once a call is answered, the called party can be replaced through call transfer or call park and retrieval, and a back-to-back user agent can hide this. The scope is signaling only, not whether media from the connected party should be rendered.
sections.eli5: Crooks can send your call to the wrong place or fake a hang-up. Signed proof from the answerer helps you catch both tricks.

sections.title: Connected Identity Without Diversion
sections.content:
In a straightforward call, the address-of-record of the party reached matches the dest field of the PASSporT in the INVITE's Identity header. If the terminating side is STIR-capable, it can sign a PASSporT for that address-of-record.

This document lets provisional and final SIP responses, including 100, 180, 183 and 200, carry an Identity header field. Their PASSporTs SHOULD use a ppt of rsp. An rsp PASSporT is signed much like a div PASSporT (RFC 8946): the certificate vouches for the dest field, not orig. If the terminating side has no credential to sign for that dest, it MUST NOT send an rsp PASSporT.

Failure responses (4XX, 5XX, 6XX) do not form dialogs and are out of scope, as are redirect (3XX) responses.

A response cannot be rejected the way a request can. A caller who gets a problem PASSporT can only send CANCEL (for a provisional dialog) or BYE. Provisional responses are not reliably delivered without 100rel and PRACK, and intermediaries may consume them, so delivery is not guaranteed.
sections.eli5: When someone picks up, they hold up a signed card with their own name on it. If they cannot sign for that name, they must not hold up a card at all.

sections.title: Connected Identity With Diversion
sections.content:
Sometimes a call is legitimately retargeted in transit, so the party reached differs from the original dest. Why should the caller trust a response signed for a different destination? The existing tool is the div PASSporT, which records a retargeting. Until now, a caller would only see one if the network used a redirect (3XX) rather than retargeting.

This document adds another route. A User Agent Server sending an rsp PASSporT MAY also include in its Identity headers any div PASSporTs it received in the INVITE. In that case, the dest signed in the rsp MUST be the address-of-record of the party actually reached.

  • An rsp that signs a different dest than the original request MUST be sent with at least one div PASSporT.
  • If no div PASSporTs came with a retargeted request, rsp MUST NOT be used.
  • Whether to trust any div or rsp is local policy; stricter systems may refuse any rsp whose dest differs from the original.

Sending div backwards can reveal service logic, so the called party can decide by policy whether to do it. Unlike RFC 4916, this mechanism does not need the From header changed, since many environments carry the asserted identity in P-Asserted-Identity (RFC 3325) instead.
sections.eli5: If your call was passed to a helper on purpose, the helper must also show the note saying who passed it along. No note, no card.

sections.title: Mid-Dialog and Dialog-Terminating Requests
sections.content:
Once a dialog has connected identity, any re-INVITE from either side, and any BYE, SHOULD carry an Identity header with a valid PASSporT. This stops third parties spoofing mid-dialog requests to redirect media and stops denial-of-service teardowns. If only the terminating side supports the mechanism, the originator cannot be expected to know to sign its later requests.

The RFC does not recommend PASSporTs for requests other than INVITE, UPDATE and BYE. Bodies of requests such as INFO and MESSAGE would need extra specification. A CANCEL cannot be required to carry one, because stateful proxies may send CANCEL when forking.

With diversion, relying parties that trust an rsp MUST validate the div chain back to it. The dialog initiator can then treat the certificate that signed the rsp as the right one for later backwards requests. The dest in those later messages MUST match the dest in the first response with a PASSporT, unless the from-change extension is used.
sections.eli5: Once you have checked who answered, they should keep signing their later messages, so nobody can fake a hang-up.

sections.title: Caller Policy and Pre-Association
sections.content:
Callers, unlike called parties, usually cannot read a screen while dialing, and their natural reaction to a security problem is to hang up. The RFC does not prescribe a user experience, but assumes callers can set a posture, per call or per destination, that makes a call fail if it reaches an unexpected or unauthenticated party. It compares this to refusing to exchange media when SRTP negotiation fails.

Connected identity works best if the caller knows beforehand that the destination supports it. The text suggests a directory that advertises support, or a device log noting that a destination used to support it. It also suggests using the moment before dialing, such as address book lookups, to probe the destination.

One way is a media-less dialog: an INVITE with an Identity header but no SDP. A STIR-aware UAS that supports this document and sees such an INVITE with a PASSporT and 100rel in the Require header SHOULD send a provisional response carrying a PASSporT, which can be shown to the user before they decide to call.
sections.eli5: Before an important call, you could ask, "Are you really the bank?" and only go on if the answer checks out.

sections.title: The rsp PASSporT Type
sections.content:
The rsp type is sent only in SIP responses. It MUST NOT be sent in requests, and any rsp PASSporT received in a request MUST be ignored.

The header shows a ppt of rsp. The payload looks like a normal PASSporT; only the meaning differs, since the signature authenticates the dest claim rather than orig. No restrictions are placed on extra payload elements.

IANA registers rsp in the Personal Assertion Token (PASSporT) Extensions registry, with a reference to Section 9 of this RFC. The RFC also notes that RFC 4916's from-change UPDATE procedure for provisional dialogs is too complex to deploy for the main use cases. It is neither deprecated nor updated for STIR, which is left for future work.
sections.eli5: It is a normal signed note, except the signature says who answered rather than who called.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
Privacy. Sending connected identity can reveal information about the called party. If they do not want to be identified, rich call data (RCD) should not be shared backwards, especially in business-to-consumer calls. Sharing must be an opt-in choice for users.

Security. The considerations of RFC 8224 and RFC 8225 apply, and an rsp has security properties similar to div. It addresses impersonated responses (route hijacking via a forged dialog-forming response) and impersonated mid-dialog or terminating requests (a forged BYE or a forged re-INVITE that negotiates attacker-controlled media). Its value depends on the relying party trusting the signing certificate and knowing it may sign for the dest number. For certificates using Service Provider Codes, the relying party learns which network operator vouches for the rsp, enabling traceback.

Putting PASSporTs in responses is a new potential amplification vector, because many responses can answer one request and a PASSporT enlarges them. The RFC argues called parties can mitigate this, since responses only carry a PASSporT when the request carried one and so came from a strongly authenticated sender.
sections.eli5: Signed proof keeps liars out, but it also tells callers a bit about the answerer, so answerers get to choose whether to share.
